122 THIRTY-THIRD REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
June 30, 1916. 
Mr. Warren J. Brown, Mr. Henry C. Mansfield, and Mrs. Florence E. Cleve￾land may be appointed as clerks in the classified service of the Government with￾out reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recom￾mendation of the Secretary of War, who submits a detailed report from the 
governor of the Panama Canal giving special reasons as to why the same should 
be issued, in view of which it is believed that the appointment of these three 
persons will be in the interest of the service. From the governor’s report it ap￾pears that Messrs. Brown and Mansfield have rendered long and very satisfac￾tory service in the employment of the Government on the Isthmus of Panama; 
and that Mrs. Cleveland, whose husband was killed May 23, 1914, while em￾ployed as an operator of one of the towing locomotives of the Panama Canal, 
has been employed in an excepted position in the Panama Canal service since 
November 16, 1914, in which position it appears she has rendered very satis￾factory service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mrs. Olivia Blanchard may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
under the Department of Labor without reference to the civil-service rules. This 
order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states 
that the department contemplates the establishment of a branch of the United 
States Employment Service in the city of New Orleans, La., and that it is neces￾sary that a woman employee be assigned thereto to attend to applications of 
women for employment or help, and it is believed that a woman as favorably 
known in New Orleans as Mrs. Blanchard is would possess advantages calcu￾lated to promote the interests of the new employment service, and that her 
acquaintance would make her services desirable in the labors of woman’s and 
girl’s division of said service involving vocational direction as to industrial 
training of girls. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mr. Marion T. Edwards may be appointed to the position of assistant messen￾ger qualified in the operation and repair of automobiles, in the Bureau of Stand￾ards at $720 per annum, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order 
is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Direc￾tor of the Bureau of Standards, who state that the position to which it is pro￾posed to appoint Mr. Edwards is a confidential post; that by experience and 
training Mr. Edwards is especially qualified for the position; and that his ap￾pointment would be in the interests of good administration. The Civil Service 
Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Miss Ruth L. O'Donnell may be appointed to a position in the Bureau of Effi￾ciency without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the 
recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Efficiency, who states that Miss 
O’Donnell has been employed in his office at various times during the past two 
years; that her services have been most satisfactory; and that her permanent 
appointment to the force of the Bureau of Efficiency would be a distinct advan￾tage to the bureau. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 18, 1916. 
Mr. Jacob P. Smith may be appointed a storekeeper-gauger in the Internal￾Revenue Service without compliance with civil-service rules. The collector of 
internal revenue for the seventh district of Indiana states that Mr. Smith served 
temporarily as a storekeeper-gauger in that district from September, 1915, until 
June 26, 1916; that he is qualified to competently fill any position in the store￾keeper-gauger service; and that his permanent appointment will be in the inter￾est of efficient administration. The collector further states that the stress of 
work at this time in his district necessitates the employment of an experienced 
man. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury. Mr. Smith is on the civil-service register. 
July 19, 1916. 
Mr, Arthur E. Wilson may be permanently appointed to a clerical position in 
the office of the Surgeon General, Public Health Service, without reference to

Mrs. Olga S. Moncure may be reinstated in the position of topographic

upon recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the superintendent 
of the survey, who state that Mrs. Moncure served satisfactorily and very 
efficiently in a statutory position of topographic draftsman in the Geological 
Survey during a period of seven years; that upon applying for a short leave 
of absence she was transferred to a position on a per diem, when actually em￾ployed, basis with the positive assurance of her superior officers that such 
transfer would not deprive her of her status in the classified civil service; 
that she did apply for restoration to duty prior to the expiration of the time 
during which she was advised that she would be eligible for such return to duty 
and then learned that she had been misinformed, and as a result of the action 
of her superiors she lost her civil-service status; that she later obtained a 
position of draftsman in the bureau of lands in the Philippines and while 
serving in that capacity was detailed for work under the director of coast 
surveys at Manila, who has certified to her faithfulness, efficiency, and atten￾tion to duty; and that in view of these circumstances it is believed that her 
reinstatement in the Coast and Geodetic Survey is fully justified and desirable 
in the interests of good administration and will remedy a manifest injustice 
which has been done in her case.

Albert W. Smith may be promoted to a subclerical position in the Treas￾ury Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is

physician, he fully recovered his health, and on November 26, 1917, was ap￾pointed a clerk in the Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice, where

This order is issued upon recommendation of the Attorney Ceneral, with the

January 12, 1922. 
Mr. Paul Bazaar may be appointed as clerk in the Rochester, N. Y., office 
of the United States Veterans’ Bureau, without examination under the civil 
service rules. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Director of the United 
States Veterans’ Bureau. Mr. Bazaar, who suffered the loss of both hands in 
the World War, has by the use of artificial hands become so rehabilitated that 
he can operate a typewriter and satisfactorily perform clerical duties. The 
case being exceptional, the director believes that his appointment would have 
a beneficial psychological effect upon the disabled ex-service men in that vicinity. 
January 25, 1922. 
Mr. Ernest W. Camp may be appointed Chief, Division of Customs, Treasury 
Department, without examination under the civil service rules. 
March 6, 1922. 
Mr. Arthur W. Mueller may be appointed to the position of clerk in the Post 
Office Department without regard to civil service rules and regulations. 
The Postmaster General recommends this order in view of Mr. Mueller’s 
satisfactory service in the Division of Air Mail Service, which service at the 
time of Mr. Mueller’s appointment was not treated as in the classified service. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
March 6, 1922. 
Mrs. Mary Asquith Hughes may be appointed to a clerical position in the 
classified service of the Government without regard to the requirements of the 
civil-service rules. 
Mrs. Hughes, who had some clerical experience prior to her marriage, is the 
widow of William G. Hughes, who was appointed to a position in the Bureau 
of Construction and Repair, Navy Department, on June 9, 1890, and continued 
in the employ of said department under various ratings until he lost his life 
in the Knickerbocker disaster on January 28, 1922, and who was considered 
by his immediate superiors and fellow workers as a most efficient employee. 
March 23, 1922. 
Thomas B. McKaig may be appointed to a permanent position in the classi￾fied service of the Treasury Department without regard to the requirements of 
the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, 
who states that Mr. McKaig has rendered distinguished service as a temporary 
valuation expert in the Valuation Investigation Division; that he has shown 
the highest qualifications for executive administrative responsibilities; and that 
his permanent appointment will be greatly in the interest of the service. 
The Cvil Service Commission did not concur in recommending the order. 
April 22, 1922. 
John M. Masten may be appointed to a position as investigator in the Gen￾eral Accounting Office without compliance with civil-service rules. Mr. Masten 
has had wide and varied experience in investigating work in the Post Office 
Department, and it is believed that in view of his qualifications and experience 
in this line of work it would be in the interest of the service to make this 
appointment. 
April 22, 1922. 
Frank H. Bogardus may be appointed to a position as investigator in the 
General Accounting Office without compliance with civil-service rules. Mr. 
Bogardus has had wide and varied experience as investigator along accounting 
lines. He was temporarily appointed as investigator, on November 16, 1921, in 
the General Accounting Office, and his services have proven entirely satisfactory

April 28, 1922. . 
Mr. Sims Ely, of Arizona, may be appointed to the position of chief clerk 
and administrative assistant, Department of Justice, without reference to the 
civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who 
states that the position of chief clerk is highly confidential and requires a 
peculiar order of talent; that a diligent effort has been made within the classi￾fied service to find some one possessing the required qualifications, but without 
success. The Attorney General believes that Mr. Ely is especially qualified 
for the position and that the interests of the service would be promoted by 
exempting the appointment. 
May 20, 1922. ; 
Mr. John E. Pitts may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service 
without regard to time limit. 
He was appointed in the Railway Mail Service September 27, 1889, and 
served continuously therein until May 2, 1903, when his resignation was ac￾cepted, for the reason that, having been severely injured on duty in a railroad 
wreck a year previous to that time and having been granted all the leave of 
absence with pay allowed by law, he was still unable to resume duty. His reinstatement is recommended by the Postmaster General in order 
that he may be given such work in the Railway Mail Service as he will be able 
to perform. 
May 24, 1922. 
The following-named employees in the Office of the Superintendent, State, 
War, and Navy Department Buildings, are transferred from an unclassified to 
a classified status without regard to the provision of civil-service rules: William 
A. Boyd, Martha Jones, Malvina Lee, Anna M. Over, John A. Simms, Lillie B. 
Sinclair, and Susan Wills. 
This order is issued on the joint recommendation of the Commission in 
Charge of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings, Lieut. Col. C. O. 
Sherrill, Superintendent of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings, 
and the Civil Service Commission, because of the employees’ long, faithful, 
and efficient service, and for the reason that they are unable to pass the required 
civil-service examinations for lack of education and training.

AMENDMENT OF FOURTH-CLASS POSTMASTER REGULATIONS
NOT TO BE EXAMINED AFTER REACHING 85 YEARS OF AGE
January 12, 1925. 
On the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission and the Postmaster
General the word "examined" is substituted for the word "appointed" in line 1
of section 7, Regulations Governing the Appointment of Postmasters of the Fourth
Class. As amended section 7 will read:
"7. No person shall be examined under the regulations of November 25, 1912,
as amended, as postmaster of an office of the fourth class where the annual
compensation is as much as $500 after he has reached his sixty-fifth birthday."
ORDERS RELATING TO EXAMINATIONS FOR PRESIDENTIAL POST
OFFICES
WAIVER OF EXAMINATION REQUIREMENT
January 8, 1925. 
Mr. A. H. Bergthold may be appointed postmaster at Weatherford, Okla.,
without regard to the Executive order of May 10, 1921, requiring candidates to
pass a civil-service examination for presidential postmasterships.
This order is issued on recommendation of the Postmaster General, who states
that Mr. Bergthold has been acting postmaster since June 5, 1923, and his service
has been satisfactory.
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order.
WAIVER OF AGE REQUIREMENT
January 10, 1925. 
Mr. Charles C. Kellogg may be admitted to the examination for postmaster at
Detroit without regard to his age.
Mr. Kellogg has been in the classified service since 1895 and, if his promotion
without examination were proposed, his age would not be a bar.
The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Postmaster General in recom￾mending this order.
ORDERS TRANSFERRING BUREAUS AND OFFICES FROM DEPART￾MENT OF THE INTERIOR TO DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE
TRANSFER OF PATENT OFFICE, DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, TO DEPARTMENT
OF COMMERCE
March 17, 1925. 
I, Calvin Coolidge, President of the United States of America, under the
authority conferred upon me by Act of February 14, 1903, entitled "An Act to
establish the Department of Commerce and Labor" (32 Stat. 826), and by virtue
of all other powers thereto me enabling, do hereby transfer from the Department
of the Interior to the Department of Commerce, to be administered under the
supervision of the Secretary of Commerce, the United States Patent Office,
together with all appropriations, the records and all public property of said service
in the District of Columbia or elsewhere, as provided in the Act of February 14,
1903, supra. The transfer above mentioned shall be effective from and including
April 1, 1925.
TRANSFER OF BUREAU OF MINES AND DIVISION OF MINERAL RESOURCES, GEOLOGICAL
SURVEY, DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR TO THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

virtue of all other powers thereto me enabling, do hereby transfer from the Depart￾ment of the Interior to the Department of Commerce, to be administered under
the supervision of the Secretary of Commerce, the Bureau of Mines and the

TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 117
The duties to be performed by Mr. Pitts in the immediate office of the Sec¬
retary of the Treasury are of a confidential nature, and require a man having
good judgment, tact, and a wide knowledge of public men. For these reasons
the President issued the order.
March 5, 1907.
James G. Massey, of Maryland, may be appointed to a clerical position in
the Department of the Interior without reference to civil-service rules.
Mr. Massey was appointed to a clerkship in the Department of Commerce and
Labor in October, 1905, and in that Department was employed on work under
the immediate direction of Commissioner James R. Garfield, at that time Com¬
missioner of Corporations. This work was of a more or less confidential nature.
Mr. Garfield, as Secretary of the Interior, desired Mr. Massey's services in the
Interior Department, but he was not eligible' for transfer by reason of the
three-year limitation imposed by statute. He therefore resigned Ms position
in the Department of Commerce and Labor and was appointed in the Interior
Department upon the order of the President.
March 7, 1907.
Mr. John C. Eversman, sr., a special examiner in the Pension Office, may be
appointed or transferred to a competitive position in that office.
Mr. Eversman was appointed as a special examiner in the Pension Office
under Schedule A of the civil-service rules, which excepts from the require¬
ment of examination five pension examiners to investigate fraudulent and other
pension claims of a criminal nature. The Commissioner of Pensions desired
to have Mr. Eversman covered into the classified service, and the Executive
order allowing this was signed by the President.
March 8, 1907.
Mr. P. J. Hughes, who was separated from the Isthmian Canal Service on
account of ill health and whose case is regarded by the Isthmian Canal Com¬
mission as particularly meritorious and deserving, may be reinstated and trans¬
ferred as a clerk to the War Department or one of its field branches.
Mr. Hughes was selected on March 16, 1905, for appointment as clerk at $75
per month on the Isthmus of Panama through the clerk examination, and was
discharged on April 27, 1906, from the position of clerk at $100 per month, the
condition of his health making such action necessary. His accumulated leave
of absence was granted him and arrangements made for the payment of his sal¬
ary in the United States while on leave, such adjustment at that time being
only authorized in exceptional and meritorious cases. The chief, office of
administration, stated that he thought Mr. Hughes’s case was deserving of
special consideration.
March 8, 1907.
Mr. C. F. House may be appointed as clerk at $1,000 per annum, Naval
Training Station, Great Lakes, North Chicago, Ill., without compliance with the
civil-service rules.
The Navy Department had endeavored to fill this vacancy through certifica¬
tion for a period extending over five months, but had been unable to do so
owing to the repeated declinations of the eligibles certified. The situation
is isolated and the cost of living in the immediate vicinity is high, and it
therefore seemed impracticable to make an appointment through certification.
Mr. House was formerly an enlisted man and a competent employee and was
willing to accept the position.

118 TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
March 15, 1907.
Dr. A. Brown may be appointed in the Department of Agriculture without
examination on account of his special ability along the line of work in execu¬
tion of tlie pure-food and drugs law.
This order was signed by the President upon the request of Secretary Wilson,
of the Department of Agriculture. The reasons for Secretary Wilson’s action
are set forth in the following letter to the President:
We are preparing to execute the pure-food and drugs law, and the Civil Serv¬
ice Commission, by examination, is securing for us the necessary officials. I
would like to have Dr. A. Brown, of Letts, Iowa, appointed by you, on account
of his special ability along the lines of work required in the execution of that
law.
He belongs to a large class of men of special ability who are reluctant to take
examinations. I am in entire accord with the Civil Service Commission and
fully approve of their supervision over entrance to the Government service.
But there are exceptions to this rule, as there are to most others, and after ten
years’ experience in the Government service I think the President might make
occasional exceptions where they will result in giving the Government the
services of high-class officials who can not be obtained in any other way. I
would not, however, regard it as safe to give this power to any other officer of
the Government.
I may add that there have been a good many men brought into the service of
this Department without examination on account of their experience and pecul¬
iar ability in certain lines. The Department has been growing rapidly, and it
was necessary quite often to do this in order that we might get men qualified
to carry on our work. The tendency has been to limit the bringing in of such
exceptional men, and I have been more and more turning to the Civil Service
Commission to find me the officials I require. My mind is to pursue that course
in the future. But there are and will be occasions where men peculiarly fitted
for certain kinds of work should be put in by you. I think it would probably
strengthen the service if several were put in for this new line of work, but this
one is all that I shall ask.

in the Department of the Interior.

March 15, 1907.
Mr. R. H. Mitchell may be appointed as a watchman without examination
in the Department of the Interior.
On August 12, 1882, prior to the passage of the civil-service act, Mr. Mitchell
was appointed as a clerk in the office of The Adjutant-General, War Depart¬
ment. Mr. Mitchell was discharged November 12, 1887. He was subsequently
employed for fifteen years as usher and ticket examiner at the Pennsylvania
Railroad station. He was strongly indorsed by a number of prominent offi¬
cials and by residents of Washington who knew him in a business capacity.
He was also strongly indorsed by the station master of the Pennsylvania
Railroad.
March 18, 1907.
Mr. Charles P. Galpin, a messenger in the Pension Office, may be appointed
to a clerical position in that office without examination.
This order was signed by the President upon the recommendation of the
Commissioner of Pensions.
March 19, 1907.
Frederick M. Kerby, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to a
clerical position in the Department of the Interior, without reference to civil￾service rules.
Mr. Kerby was appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of Corporations
February, 1906, and was employed upon work of a more or less confidential
nature under the immediate supervision of Commissioner Garfield. As Secre¬
tary of the Interior Mr. Garfield desired his services. As the statute requiring
three years’ service in one Department before transfer to another prevented

TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 119
Mr. Kerby’s transfer, be resigned from the Department of Commerce and Labor
and was appointed in the Interior Department upon Executive order.
March 19, 1907.
Harlan Updegraff, of Iowa, may be appointed Alaskan assistant under the
Bureau of Education without reference to civil-service rules.
Mr. Updegraff had had valuable and very successful experience as teacher
and superintendent of schools in the States of Iowa and Maryland, and it wras
desired to utilize his services as an assistant to the Commissioner of Educa¬
tion in the reorganization of the work of the Alaska division. At the time of
his appointment he was a graduate student of Columbia University and a
candidate for the degree of doctor of philosophy. He was highly recommended
by President Nicholas Murray Butler and Dean James E. Russell, of Colum¬
bia University.
March 23, 1907.
Mr. Mahlon Pursel may be reinstated as a clerk in the Adjutant-General’s
Office, War Department, without reference to the time limit of eligibility for
reinstatement under the civil-service rules.
The Commission was not Informed of the reasons for the promulgation of
this order.
March 25, 1907.
Mr. F. T. Quinlan may be reinstated as an inspector of furs in the quarter¬
master's department at Philadelphia, Pa.
Mr. Quinlan was appointed as a laborer November 1, 1900, in the quartermas¬
ter’s department, Philadelphia, Pa., and under that designation was employed
as a fur inspector. He was removed from the service September 16, 1905, be¬
cause when the inspector questioned him during the course of an investigation
of certain frauds discovered in the arsenal, he refused to answer on the ground
that his integrity was impugned. The quartermaster stated that Mr. Quinlan
was not guilty of any irregularities and circumstances in the case were such
as to call for exceptional action in his behalf. Had Mr. Quinlan remained in
the service he would have been classified by the Executive order of February
24, 1906.
General Mulholland says: “As a soldier, you will understand my interest in
the matter when I tell you that Major Quinlan, who was then a lieutenant in
my regiment, at the battle of Fredericksburg saved the colors by his personal
heroism.”
The Commission recommended the issuance of the Executive order.
March 26, 1907.
Mrs. Theresa S. Aubright may he appointed to a clerical position in the
classified civil service without examination.

134 TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
July 2, 1908.
Mr. Joe M. Johnson may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation therefrom.
Mr. Johnson served continuously in the Government Printing Office as a com¬
positor and proof reader from February 7, 1899, to November 20, 1905, and
inasmuch as he had been separated from the service for more than one year the
commission was without authority to issue a certificate for his reinstatement.

petitive classified service on account of the confidential relationship, more or less personal in character, which existed between the superintendent of the mint and his cashier. The Commission subsequently concurred in recommending that cashiers at the smaller assay offices be made competitive, as their duties did not differ essen- tially from those of chief clerks, as all payments in such offices were made by check as they are now. At present no cashiers except those in the Mint Service are excepted from examination. The Director of the Mint certified that all these men were selected on account of their known qualifications, that their records are unblemished and their abilities have been fully demonstrated. Paragraph 3, Subdivision VII, Schedule A of the civil-service rules, excepting one private secretary or confidential clerk to the postmaster, if authorized by the Post￾master General, at each post office where the receipts of the last preceding fiscal year amounted to as much as $350,000, is hereby stricken out and the following paragraphs will be renumbered accordingly, the position of private secretary in the post-office gervice having ceased to exist. 
MISCELLANEOUS ORDERS. 
EMPLOYMENT OF MEXICANS AS A MATTER OF COMITY. 
November 6, 1911. 
Such alumni of the National School of Engineering of Mexico as may be designated 
by the Mexican Government to observe certain public works in the United States and Panama may be employed under the several executive departments of the United States in connection with the works to which they may be assigned. This order is issued in accordance with the principles of international comity to permit the action desired by the Mexican Government. As the matter is one relating 
to international courtesy rather than to the interests of the executive civil service, the Civil Service Commission makes no recommendation, regarding the wisdom of the proposed waiver as a matter pertaining to the departments concerned. 
REINSTATEMENT OF PERSONS WHO RESIGN TO BECOME CANDIDATES FOR OFFICE OR TO 
ENGAGE IN ACTIVE POLITICAL WORK. 
December 26, 1911. 
On December 21, 1911, the commission presented to the President, with request 
for instruction, a case involving action under the following provision of minute 1 of August 10, 1908, which met with the approval of President Roosevelt: 
Inasmuch as the issuance of a certificate is discretionary with the commission, no certificate will be issued in any case where the party applying for reinstatement has previously resigned with a view of running for office, or with a view of indulging in a
next_page_text:
REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISsIoN. 1387 
degree of political activity which would be prohibited if he had remained in the service, and who afterwards, having failed in his candidacy or having indulged in the contemplated political activity, seeks reinstatement. 
The following reply has been received: 
Tre WaITE HoUsE, Washington, December 26, 1911. 
GENTLEMEN: I have your letter of December 21, and answer your question cate- gorically. I am of opinion that in accord with the spirit of our institutions in recognizing the fundamental right of citizenship, a citizen who resigns to become a candidate for office and pursues a course free from coercion, bribery, or other scandalous or unlawful conduct should not thereby be prejudiced by being refused reinstatement within the period of eligibility prescribed by the rules; nor do I think any distinction should be made between the person who resigns and becomes a candidate and one who resigns, not to be a nN Gy but to manage or take part in a political campaign for a party. If he wishes to run the risk of finding an Executive who will reinstate him, and he resigns in order to avoid a violation of the rules as to participation in electoral 
contests by members of the classified service, I do not see why it should demoralize the service to allow him to resign and run the risk of securing the approval of his reinstatement by the Executive within a year after he has resigned. For that reason, I think that Mr. Max Bernfeld, who resigned his position October 20, 1911, to become a candidate for the New York Assembly, ought to be reinstated. Sincerely yours, Wu. H. Tarr. Tae Crvi. SERVICE COMMISSION, Wa hington, D. C.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 139 
The opinion of the President conveyed in the letter of his Secretary will be treated as an Executive order. (Minute 1, Mar. 23, 1912.) 
PETITIONS TO CONGRESS BY CIVIL-SERVICE EMPLOYEES, 
April 8, 1912.1 
It is hereby ordered that petitions or other communications regarding public busi- ness addressed to Congress or either House or any committee or Member thereof by officers or employees in the civil service of the United States shall be transmitted through the heads of their respective departments or offices, who shall forward them without delay with such comment as they may deem requisite in the public interest. Officers and employees are strictly prohibited either directly or indirectly from at- tempting to secure legislation, or to influence pending legislation, except in the manner above prescribed. This order supersedes the Executive orders of January 31, 1902, January 25, 1906, and November 26, 1909, regarding the same general matter 
EXCEPTIONS IN MACHINE SHOP OF THE BUREAU OF THE CENSUS. 
August 21, 1812. - 
With a view to meeting emergencies in the machine shop of the Bureau of the Census, in connection with the continuation of the Thirteenth Decennial Census work during the fiscal year 1913, the Secretary of Commerce and Labor is hereby authorized to employ, until June 30, 1913, without reference to the civil-service rules, such machinists, toolmakers, electricians, and apprentice boys (machinists) as may be necessary for the prosecution of the work whenever, in his opinion, it is not prac- ticable to make such appointments from the civil-service lists. This order extends the authority for similar appointments contained in the Executive order of December 29, 1909. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the department in recommending this order, in view of the representations of the department as to its necessity. ! 
EMPLOYMENT IN PENSION OFFICE OF FORMER TREASURY EMPLOYEES. 
August 24, 1912. 
The Commissioner of Pensions is directed to employ as extra clerks under the appro- priation of $300,000 carried in the sundry civil act approved August 24, 1912, the 30 persons heretofore employed in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Depart- ment whose names are on the list furnished to the President in a letter of the Secre- tary of the Treasury dated August 22, 1912, said appropriation act authorizing the Commissioner of Pensions to employ clerks heretofore employed in other departments of the Government service. All of these persons except one have a competitive classified status and will be eligible for reinstatement in the Treasury Department under the civil-service rules. 
MODERATOR OF A TOWN MEETING MAY BE A CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEE, 
August 24, 1912. 
The temporary office of moderator of a town meeting and offices of a like character are hereby excepted from the operation of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting persons in the Federal civil service from holding office under the charter or ordinances of any municipal corporation, and may be held by persons in the execu- tive civil service. Membership in the civil service ought not to prevent an employee from taking part in the ordinary municipal affairs of the community in which he lives, where that part does not involve permanent service but only such a temporary duty as that of acting as chairman of a municipal business meeting, where such service is not compensated by any salary or other emolument, and where the attention required by such service does not interfere with the regular and efficient discharge of the duties of the Federal office held. In the exercise of the privilege granted by this order officers and employees must not neglect their official duties and must not engage in national, State, or county political activity in violation of the civil-service rules; and in seeking the local offices named or in performing the duties thereof employees shall not use the authority or influence of their Federal positions nor take an active part in political management or 
 
in political campaigns.

CLASSIFICATION OF POSITION OF SPECIAL EMPLOYEE, INTERNAL-REVENUE SERVICE. 
August 24, 1912. 
The position of special employee in the Internal-Revenue Service shall hereafter be regarded as classified under the civil-service act and rules. No such special employee now serving shall be regarded as classified hereunder or shall acquire any right of promotion or transfer under the rules unless he is specially commended therefor by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, because of efficient services rendered, and whose name is embraced in the is furnished to the Civil Service Commission by the Treasury Department of this 
ate. The Treasury Department may make appointments of special employees for a period not exceeding 30 days or not exceeding 45 days in any one quarter of any fiscal year without reference to the civil-service rules. This order shall take effect October 1, 1912, and is issued with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Civil Service Commission. 
CLASSIFICATION AUTHORIZED OF CERTAIN EXPERTS IN THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRI- CULTURE. August 26, 1912. 
Not exceeding 115 persons appointed as experts and agents without examination under Subdivision IX, section 1 of Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, and who now are engaged upon work similar to that of competitive employees, and who are especially recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture because of their proved capacity for efficient service may be transferred to appropriate competitive positions in the Department of Agriculture. By Executive order of this date the provision of the civil-service rules permitting the appointment of agents and experts of the Department of Agriculture without examination is amended to fix more definitely the conditions under which appoint- ments can be made. This order will thus permit the classification of efficient em- ployees who can not be properly regarded as agents or experts under the amended procedure. Many of these persons are college graduates and, having been appointed at a time when agricultural colleges had not developed courses of study along certain technical lines pursued by the department, have become technologists and experts while engaged in the work of the department. The Civil Service Commission recommends this order.

March 26, 1912. 
Mr. J. C. Wilson may be reinstated as storekeeper-gauger in the Internal Revenue Service without regard to the length of time that he has been separated from the service. Mr. Wilson served from July, 1893, to December 31, 1908, as a deputy collector and storekeeper-gauger in the eighth internal revenue district of Kentucky. It appears that no vacancy occurred to which Mr. Wilson could be appointed during his period of eligibility, and on March 19, 1910, when the department requested a certificate for his reinstatement, the year of eligibility had expired and the commission was accord- ingly without authority to approve the reinstatement. The department now recom- mends the reinstatement of Mr. Wilson on the ground of his long and efficient service, his well-established good character and the need of the collector for the services of such an officer, stating that the service would be benefited by Mr. Wilson’s appoint￾ment. 
In view of the facts above stated, the commission joins with the department in rec- ommending an Executive order. 
March 30, 1912. 
Mr. Andrew M. Latham may be appointed to the position of clerk in the Depart- ment of Agriculture without reference to the provisions of the civil-service rules. Mr. Latham passed the civil-service examination and received certification and appointment to a temporary clerkship in the Department of Agriculture. Circum- stances are such that he would probably not be reached for certification for permanent appointment. 
The Secretary of Agriculture states that Mr. Latham is a young man of 27 years of age, of good habits, industrious, and thoroughly efficient; that he is crippled, having been deprived of the use of his limbs, but in all other respects is of good physique and of exceptional good health. The order is based on the ground that the Secretary of Agriculture recommends such action in the interest of the public service. It is not intended to form a prece- dent that because one is a cripple he is entitled to a waiver of the regulations of the civil-service law. The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in the recom- mendation. . 
March 30, 1912. 
Mr. Y. Tsenshan Wang may be appointed as a field assistant with a geological party during the coming field season. 
This appointment is authorized upon the request of the Chinese minister, His Excel- lency Chang Yintang, as a matter of courtesy and in accordance with the practice of the Geological Survey of maintaining friendly relations with the scientists of other nations. 
It appears from letters from Prof. J. F. Kemp, of Columbia University, and Prof. T. C. Chamberlin, of the University of Chicago, under whom Mr. Wang has pursued courses of study, that he is well qualified for the position. 
The Civil Service Commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recom- mending the issuance of the order. 
April 9, 1912. 
Miss Margaret C. Leonard may be appointed as a clerk in the War Department with- out reference to the civil-service rules involved. Miss Leonard passed the clerk examination and is on the eligible register from the District of Columbia, but in view of her standing on that register and of the fact that the District has received a number of appointments greatly in excess of its share under the apportionment, the probability that her name would be reached for appoint- ment is very remote. The Secretary of War recommends her appointment, stating that she is the daughter of Mrs. Margaret Leonard, a Union soldier’s widow, who has been employed for over 20 years in the Adjutant General’s Office but who, by reason of illness, will probably never be able to resume her work, and that the salary of the mother is the sole support of the two women. The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in the recommendation of the Secretary of War for the issuance of an Executive order,

146 REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
April 22,1912. 
Having considered the written arguments for and against the application for rein- statement of Charles H. Quackenbush in the Railway Mail Service, and having 
reached a conclusion that the offense for which Mr. Quackenbush was removed does not merit more of a penalty than a suspension without pay for a year, and that such penalty has been satisfied, I hereby direct that Mr. Quackenbush may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without reference to the provisions of the civil-service rule governing reinstatements. This order 1s made without the approval or disapproval of the Civil Service Com- mission and against the recommendation of the Postmaster General. 
April 30, 1912. 
Commander Homer C. Poundstone, United States Navy, retired, may be employed on the rolls of the United States Civil Service Commission without examination under the civil-service rules. This action is taken at the request of the Civil Service Commission because of his peculiar and exceptional qualifications and his high and recognized attainments. 
May 10, 1912. 
Miss Louise Lester may be appointed a clerk in the classified executive civil service without compliance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued for the reason that it is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury so that Miss Lester may be appointed a special witness of the destruction of United States securities in the Treasury Department, it being the Secretary’s judgment that Miss Lester possesses special qualifications which will render her par- ticularly desirable as a member of the destruction committee. 
May 27, 1912. 
Mr. Walter L. Barnum may be reinstated to an appropriate clerical position in the classified service without regard to the length of his separation therefrom. Mr. Barnum resigned from the competitive position of clerk in the Post Office Department on February 19, 1908. Since that time he has oso the examination in stenography and typewriting with a high grade, and has eveloped the qualifica- tions of an expert clerk during his service in an excepted position in the Post Office Department from April 1, 1909, to the present time. In view of his high rating and his record as an expert clerk, the commission joins with the Postmaster General in recommending the order.
